notes.meaning: God commands Moses to build a special wooden altar made of durable acacia wood. Its only purpose is for burning fragrant spices before the Lord, not for killing animal sacrifices. The sweet smell rising from it reminded the people that their worship and prayers were pleasing to God.

The altar was to be square, measuring about eighteen inches on each side and three feet high. Corner points shaped like horns were carved directly into the wood so that the whole structure formed a single solid piece. This was much smaller than the outside altar where large animal sacrifices were made.

Every part of the altar, including its flat top, all four sides, and its horns, was to be covered with pure gold. A small decorative gold border or molding was set around the top edge to keep the hot coals and spices from slipping off. Because it was placed near God's presence, only the most precious metal was fitting.

Gold rings were placed on opposite sides below the rim to hold long carrying poles. Like the altar itself, these poles were carved from acacia wood and plated with pure gold. This allowed the priests to transport the sacred furniture during Israel's travels without ever touching the altar with their bare hands.

The golden altar was to stand in the Holy Place, right in front of the heavy curtain that hid the Ark of the Covenant. Even though the priest could not see the Ark or the mercy seat through the curtain, he offered incense facing directly toward God's throne of grace. It was the piece of furniture closest to God's special meeting place with His people.

Aaron the high priest was told to burn fragrant incense on this altar twice every day, in the morning and at dusk. These times matched when he trimmed and lit the golden lamps, as well as the times of daily sacrifices. The steady rising smoke was an ongoing picture of God's people sending up their daily prayers and praises.

God strictly forbade burning any foreign incense, meaning any blend not made according to His exact recipe. The altar was also never to be used for animal sacrifices, grain gifts, or pouring out wine. It had one holy purpose, showing that God must be approached only in the way He has commanded.

Once every year, on the Day of Atonement, the high priest wiped blood from a special sacrifice on the horns of the incense altar. Atonement means covering over sins so that people are reconciled to God. This yearly cleansing reminded Israel that even their prayers and holy places needed to be purified by sacrificial blood.

Whenever the leaders counted the people of Israel, every man counted had to pay a ransom price to the Lord for his life. Counting the nation was a serious matter because Israel belonged to God, not to any human ruler. Giving this payment protected the community from falling under a deadly sickness or plague.

Each person counted was required to give a standard half-shekel of silver, weighed against an official weight kept in the sanctuary. Coined money did not exist yet, so this was a small, weighed piece of silver. The gift was presented directly as a holy offering to the Lord.

Every man twenty years old or older had to pay this exact same amount. The wealthy were not permitted to give more, and the poor were not permitted to give less. This taught that every human life has equal value before God, and every soul needs the exact same price of redemption.

The silver collected from the census was set aside to support the building and daily care of the tabernacle tent. It was used to make the heavy silver bases that supported the walls, so the ransom money visibly held up the sanctuary. This remained an ongoing reminder to the people that they were saved and kept by God's mercy.

The Lord told Moses to make a large bronze washing basin, set on its own bronze base. It stood out in the courtyard between the altar of sacrifice and the door of the holy tent. The basin was kept full of water so that the priests could clean themselves before doing God's work.

Aaron and his sons were required to wash their hands and feet before stepping into the tent or offering sacrifices at the bronze altar. Failing to wash carried the severe warning that the priest would die. Washing hands and feet pictured pure actions and a holy walk before a spotless God.

This rule of washing hands and feet was a lasting law for Aaron and his family through all future generations. It showed that God's ministers must always approach Him with clean lives. While the outward washing lasted through the Old Testament, it pointed to the inward spiritual cleansing every worshipper needs.

God gave Moses a specific recipe made of four top-grade spices mixed into about a gallon of olive oil. The spices included liquid myrrh, fragrant cinnamon, sweet-smelling cane, and cassia bark, all weighed out carefully. These were rare and costly ingredients from distant lands, chosen to create an extraordinary perfume.

A skilled perfume maker was to blend these ingredients together into a sacred anointing oil. This rich oil was set apart exclusively for God's holy use, not for everyday grooming. Anointing in the Bible often pictured the gift and setting apart of God's Holy Spirit for service.

Moses was instructed to pour this oil over the tabernacle tent, the Ark of the Covenant, and all the sacred furniture and tools. This included the bread table, the golden lampstand, both altars, and the bronze basin. Touching each object with the special oil marked it as entirely devoted to the service of God.

Anointing these objects made them most holy, completely set apart from common life. From that moment on, anything or anyone that touched them had to be holy as well. This taught Israel deep reverence for the sacred things of God's house.

Moses was also told to pour the oil upon Aaron and his sons to dedicate them to God. This anointing consecrated them, which means it officially set them apart to serve as priests. They could not minister in God's presence until this sacred mark of dedication was upon them.

The people were told that this special oil belonged only to the Lord across all future generations. It could never be splashed on an ordinary person like everyday cologne, nor could anyone copy its recipe for personal use. Anyone who copied it or poured it on an outsider was cut off, meaning separated from God's people or put to death.

God gave a recipe for the holy incense, using equal parts of four fragrant gums and spices: stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense. A skilled perfumer was to mix them together with salt, keeping the blend pure and sacred. Salt added seasoning and helped the incense burn cleanly before God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient translations like the Septuagint and Latin Vulgate rendered the word for salt as 'tempered together' or thoroughly blended, though most modern Hebrew scholars agree it means seasoned with salt.

notes.meaning: Some of this incense was to be ground into a fine powder and placed in the tabernacle right near the Ark of the Covenant. Crushing it small allowed it to catch fire easily and send up a sweet cloud of smoke when placed on the hot coals. Because it stood right where God met His people, it was considered most holy.

The Israelites were warned never to make this incense blend for their own homes or to enjoy its sweet scent. Anyone who copied the formula for private pleasure was to be cut off from the covenant community. God's sacred worship belongs to Him alone and must never be treated as everyday entertainment.
